planting.note: Plant a container-grown tree in spring after frost risk passes, in full sun with well-drained soil; protect young trees their first two winters, since the root system is hardier than the top growth and will often resprout after a hard freeze.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun after frost risk passes; Homestead is a South Florida dooryard guava selected for reliable production and good fruit quality in a home-garden setting, bearing medium-sized fruit with yellow skin and pink-tinged, sweet-tart flesh that is popular for fresh eating and for guava paste and juice alike. Like other guavas it fruits on new wood, so an annual late-winter prune keeps the shrub-form tree productive and manageable in size rather than letting it grow into an unwieldy small tree. Guava roots generally tolerate brief dips into the upper 20s Fahrenheit even when the canopy is killed back, so zone 9 gardeners should mulch the root zone heavily going into winter and expect to prune out and regrow frozen top growth in a hard year. In a favorable year with a long warm season, established plants can produce two overlapping flushes of fruit.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Guava Growing in the Home Landscape
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Guava Production Guide

planting.note: Plant a container-grown tree in spring after frost risk passes, in full sun with well-drained soil; Frostproof is a more cold-tolerant, smaller-statured guava selection that some Gulf South gardeners can grow in-ground in protected zone 9 microclimates.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun after frost risk passes; Frostproof is a compact, shrubby guava cultivar selected for better cold tolerance than standard tropical guava types, making it one of the more realistic guava choices for in-ground planting at the cooler edge of guava-growing range. Fruit is smaller than many named guava cultivars but still sweet and fragrant, with pink-blushed flesh good for fresh eating and preserves. Because it stays more compact than most guavas even at maturity, Frostproof also works well trained as a large container specimen that can be moved under cover during a hard freeze. As with other guavas, root hardiness exceeds top-growth hardiness, so established plants generally resprout from the base after a freeze that kills the canopy; mulch the root zone heavily each winter and prune out dead wood once new growth confirms which stems survived.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Guava Growing in the Home Landscape
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Guava Production Guide

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in well-drained soil, or grow in a large container to shelter from frost; Julie's dwarf, compact habit and Caribbean popularity make it a favorite dooryard mango where space and winter protection are both limited.

directions: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in well-drained soil, or grow in a large container to move under cover before frost; Julie is a small, dwarf-habit mango of Caribbean origin, especially beloved in Jamaican and Trinidadian dooryard gardens for its compact size, precocious bearing, and intensely sweet, fiberless, deep orange flesh with a distinctive rich flavor that fans consider among the best of any mango. Because it stays notably smaller than most mango cultivars, Julie is one of the better choices for zone 9 gardeners growing mango in a large container that can be sheltered through winter rather than risking an in-ground planting. Reduce irrigation as fruit nears ripeness to concentrate sugars and flavor, and protect trees from any frost, since even brief freezing temperatures can damage or kill mango wood.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Mango Growing in the Home Landscape
Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden — Mango Cultivar Notes

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in well-drained soil, or grow in a large container to shelter from frost; Pickering is a compact Florida-bred mango prized for consistent, heavy bearing on a manageable-sized tree.

directions: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in well-drained soil, or grow in a large container to move under cover before frost; Pickering is a Florida-bred mango descended from Alampur Baneshan, developed as a compact, heavy-bearing dooryard cultivar for home gardeners with limited space. Fruit is medium-sized with a rich, sweet, aromatic, fiberless flesh and a flavor many growers rank among the best of the Florida dooryard mangoes, ripening over a fairly long summer window that extends the harvest compared to single-flush cultivars. Its naturally compact size and tendency toward heavy annual bearing make it a strong choice for zone 9 gardeners planning to grow mango in a large container that can be sheltered through winter. Reduce watering as fruit approaches ripeness to concentrate flavor, and protect the tree from any frost or freeze, since mango wood is damaged even by brief cold snaps.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Mango Growing in the Home Landscape
Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden — Mango Cultivar Notes

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in well-drained soil, or grow in a large container to shelter from frost; Fairchild's small, dense, dwarf-tending habit makes it one of the easiest mangoes to keep manageable in a container in zone 9.

directions: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in well-drained soil, or grow in a large container to move under cover before frost; Fairchild is a Panama-origin mango named for plant explorer David Fairchild and grown widely in South Florida dooryards for its small, dense, naturally dwarf-tending habit that suits small yards and container culture better than most mango cultivars. Fruit is small to medium with mild, sweet, fiberless flesh and a gentle flavor that is a good introduction to mango for those used to only supermarket varieties. The tree's compact growth and tolerance for hedging or pruning make it especially practical for zone 9 gardeners who want to keep a container specimen small enough to move indoors or into a greenhouse before winter cold arrives. Reduce irrigation as fruit ripens to concentrate flavor and protect the tree from any frost, since mango wood is damaged even by brief cold exposure.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Mango Growing in the Home Landscape
